item.title: Lithuania's political gamble comes at too high a price: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 00:34:00
Lithuania Illustration: Chen Xia/GT Recently, media reports said Lithuania's foreign affairs department is pushing to change the name of the "Taiwan Representative Office." Since the beginning of this year, Lithuania has been floating signals about "restoring diplomatic relations with China." Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda has acknowledged that setting up the "Taiwan Representative Office" was a mistake, and the new government has set a goal of normalizing diplomatic relations with China. But beyond that, we have so far not seen more concrete steps from Lithuania to improve the situation. Five years ago, Lithuania's previous government crossed China's red line on the Taiwan question. Disregarding China's solemn protests, it openly allowed the Taiwan authorities to establish a so-called representative office under the name "Taiwan," deliberately creating the false impression of "one China, one Taiwan." This move seriously undermined the political foundation of China-Lithuania relations and made Lithuania an outlier among EU member states in their relations with China. Yet Vilnius gravely underestimated China's capacity for strategic countermeasures. Before bilateral relations deteriorated in 2021, practical economic and trade cooperation had kept bilateral trade on an upward trend for an extended period, reaching a historic high in 2020. Following the deterioration of relations, however, economic and trade cooperation suffered a comprehensive downturn. The harsh realities of the past five years have demonstrated that abandoning the one-China principle and openly supporting the Taiwan authorities haven't benefited Lithuania. Instead, they have damaged its economy and left it diplomatically disadvantaged. Clearly, Lithuania's current government is unwilling to continue shouldering the burden of this disastrous legacy. Yet it remains hesitant and indecisive when it comes to addressing the fundamental issue of correcting its mistakes. For example, while signaling its hope to "put bilateral relations back on track," it has simultaneously claimed that it is "too early" to discuss renaming the so-called "Taiwan Representative Office." To some extent, the current government's hope to mend ties with China has been driven by Lithuania's difficult domestic economic situation and public opinion. A Lithuanian survey conducted this year shows that nearly 60 percent of Lithuanians have recognized the illusory nature and enormous costs of attempting to "use Taiwan to contain China," and want their government to repair relations with China and abandon opportunistic political maneuvering. However, Vilnius still clings to illusions about the empty promises made by certain Western actors and the flattering labels of "democracy" they have bestowed upon it. That is why Lithuania continues to hold on to this political hot potato, despite the discomfort it causes. This also suggests that Lithuania may not yet be prepared for the normalization of relations with China. The one-China principle is a widely recognized norm governing international relations and a broad consensus of the international community. It also constitutes the political foundation of China-Lithuania and China-EU relations. Anti-China forces in the West have sought to turn Lithuania into a strategic pawn in their geopolitical maneuvering, encouraging it to play the "Taiwan card" to provoke China. Such underhanded tactics, which tie the interests of smaller countries to great-power rivalry for the benefits of others, will ultimately leave those smaller countries bearing the consequences and suffering a backlash. Lithuania's prolonged and costly detour has made this reality even clearer to the international community. It must be noted that renaming the Taiwan-related representative office is an inevitable trend, and such a change would be only the first step, not the final destination, in Lithuania's efforts to correct its mistakes. Even if Lithuania changes the erroneous name of the so-called "Taiwan Representative Office," this would not mean that its relations with China could immediately "return to the past." Nor should Vilnius attempt to use the proposed name change as a bargaining chip in negotiations with China. The Taiwan question is China's internal affair and the core of China's core interests. There is no room for compromise or concession. What Lithuania needs to do is bring its foreign policy fully into alignment with the one-China principle. Only then can bilateral relations potentially resume practical cooperation, and only then can Lithuania truly move beyond its past strategic dilemma. The one-China principle is a binding constraint, not an optional choice. Any separatist attempt to play the "Taiwan card" or engage in word games over names will inevitably run up against the solid wall of the one-China principle. The higher one jumps, the harder the impact. All parties should have a clear understanding of this reality: Any attempt to play the "Taiwan card" for opportunistic political gains or engage in political gambling is doomed to fail. China is open to communication, but Lithuania must also demonstrate the right attitude toward dialogue. We hope Lithuania will correct its mistakes as soon as possible, honor the political commitments it made in the communiqué on the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries, and return to the right path of adhering to the one-China principle. It should translate its stated willingness to improve bilateral relations into concrete actions, thereby creating the conditions for the normalization of China-Lithuania relations. In particular, certain Lithuanian politicians should refrain from political opportunism on this fundamental matter of principle. Otherwise, no matter how many signals they send expressing a "desire to restore relations," such statements will amount to nothing more than empty gestures.

item.title: E.China's Ningbo-Zhoushan Port throughput exceeds 40m TEUs for 2nd consecutive year
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 23:18:00
A view of Ningbo-Zhoushan Port Photo: Courtesy of?Ningbo-Zhoushan?Port On Tuesday, Ningbo-Zhoushan Port in East China's Zhejiang Province, one of China's busiest ports in terms of cargo throughput, announced that its container throughput so far this year has already surpassed 40 million 20-foot equivalent units (TEUs), the second consecutive year the port has crossed the milestone of 40 million TEUs, the port told the Global Times on Tuesday. This year's achievement came 22 days earlier than last year, according to the port authorities. In 2025, Ningbo-Zhoushan Port handled more than 1.4 billion tons of cargo, ranking first globally for the 17th consecutive year. Backed by more than 220 deepwater berths for vessels of 10,000 tons and above, as well as the world's only dual "10-million-TEU-class" single-container-terminal cluster, Ningbo-Zhoushan Port is a crucial artery for exporting high-value goods, from electric vehicles and photovoltaic modules to power batteries. Meanwhile, imports of fresh products, industrial parts and other materials continue to flow into the port. "In the third quarter, vessel berth efficiency improved 4.5 percent year-on-year," Lian Sheng, director of the port's dispatching center, told the Global Times on Tuesday. "In September alone, the port handled an average of more than 140,000 TEUs per day, while monthly throughput reached 4.27 million TEUs, the highest level in the port's history." The achievement comes as China's foreign trade continues to expand steadily. The General Administration of Customs (GAC) said on Tuesday that China's total goods trade in the first 10 months of 2026 reached 44.81 trillion yuan ($6.67 trillion), up 20 percent year-on-year. Imports surged 23.6 percent, while exports rose 17.6 percent, GAC data showed. Expanding trade and a shift toward higher-value exports have brought more cargo to the port while increasing demand for faster, more reliable transport links, Lian said. Ningbo-Zhoushan Port operates more than 310 container shipping routes, connecting more than 200 countries and regions and more than 700 ports worldwide. Its port connectivity index ranks second globally, reflecting the scale and reach of its maritime network, according to the port authorities. From short-sea routes in Southeast Asia to long-haul services to Europe and the Americas, and from conventional shipping corridors to innovative logistics express lines, the port's web of connections continues to widen. This year the Arctic shipping route became a new highlight. The China-Europe Arctic Express route entered regular weekly operation starting August 15 . The route has completed eight voyages during the navigation season. The route connects Ningbo-Zhoushan Port with major European ports via the Northeast Passage and takes about 20 days, nearly half the time required by the traditional Suez Canal route. To handle growing volumes, the port has upgraded infrastructure, including deepwater shorelines, specialized berths, and cargo collection and distribution facilities. According to the port authorities, the number of sea express routes starting from Ningbo-Zhoushan Port has climbed to 28, further extending the port's transportation and service network. Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times on Tuesday that the rising throughput of Ningbo-Zhoushan Port reflects the steady rhythm of China's supply chains, the expanding global reach of its manufacturing sector, and the continued strength of the country's foreign trade. item.title: Manila becomes a testing ground for Japan to break through postwar defense constraints
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 23:11:00
Japan, the Philippines Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT The Philippines has emerged as the latest testing ground for Japan's attempts to extend its military network overseas under the guise of "security aid." According to Japanese and Philippine media reports, Japan on Monday agreed to provide radar systems to the Philippine Navy and surveillance and reconnaissance drones to its air force, which is worth 4.3 billion yen ($27.2 million), representing Japan's largest Official Security Assistance (OSA) grant to date. Jiji Press reported that this marks the first transfer of a complete defense equipment system under the framework. Previously, assistance was limited to dual-use products and parts. It is also reported that Tokyo is considering replicating this practice to other countries. From dual-use components to complete defense systems, the boundaries governing Japan's overseas transfers of military equipment are being pushed back. Wang Qiang, a Chinese military expert, noted that Japan's provision of radar systems and drones to the Philippines is a significant departure from its "exclusively defense-oriented" policy, potentially paving the way for the future transfer of lethal weapons. This is not an isolated assistance project, but part of Japan's broader efforts to break through its postwar defense constraints and expand its military capabilities. In recent years, Japan has accelerated the development of offensive weapons and revised limits on defense equipment exports, while loudly advocating for the building of bilateral and multilateral security networks with so-called "like-minded countries." By leveraging the US alliance network in the Asia-pacific region, Japan seeks to rally partners, strengthen military coordination, elevate its position in the regional security architecture and extend its military influence. The Philippines, both a US treaty ally and a long-standing economic partner of Japan, has naturally become an ideal foothold for this strategy. As part of Tokyo's broader strategic push, defense cooperation between Japan and the Philippines is deepening. The two countries have reportedly agreed to begin talks on a deal that would allow Tokyo to provide used destroyers to Manila's navy. What is presented as security cooperation is increasingly becoming a convenient channel for Japan to loosen its postwar military constraints and re-establish an overseas military presence. The greater concern lies in the wider military network Japan is seeking to build through these equipment provisions. Wang noted that Japan occupies a key position at the northern end of the First Island Chain, while the Philippines is an important strategic foothold at its southern end. By supplying radar systems and drones, Japan is helping the Philippines strengthen its maritime and aerial surveillance and intelligence-gathering capabilities, while facilitating the integration of relevant information into Japan's and potentially the US military's intelligence networks in the western Pacific. This could potentially strengthen surveillance of Chinese naval and air activities. In other words, Japan is not simply supplying a few pieces of equipment; it is using partner countries to construct a more targeted regional military cooperation network. The expansion of this military network is hardly a recipe for greater regional security. Japan repeatedly claims to be safeguarding regional peace, yet its actions involve drawing countries into closer military alignment and introducing new variables into an already sensitive security environment. What gives a country that continues to export military equipment and build military networks the right to present itself as a guardian of regional stability? Lü Chao, a Chinese expert on Northeast Asian affairs at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times that Japan used Official Development Assistance (ODA) to support the economic and social development of neighboring developing countries in the past. Today, however, Japan is increasingly using OSA to export defense equipment overseas. The name on the aid package has changed, but the logic of Japan's military expansion is becoming increasingly apparent. Established in 2023, OSA provides a new vehicle for Japan to give its militarist legacy a fresh overseas foothold under the guise of security cooperation, pushing the Asia-Pacific further toward military tensions. Today's "first" could soon become tomorrow's precedent. If Japan's defense transfers begin with radar systems and drones, what might come next under the guise of "security assistance"? When a country repeatedly repackages the dismantling of its postwar constraints as "policy innovation" and dresses up military expansion as a contribution to regional stability, the international community has little reason to continue giving it the benefit of the doubt.

item.title: GT Voice: India should embrace advanced clean tech to curb air pollution
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 21:24:00
Early morning smog engulfs the capital city after Diwali celebrations, on November 9, 2026 in New Delhi, India. Photo: VCG The Diwali fireworks have faded, but the smog over New Delhi has lingered. On Sunday, India's capital recorded a 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of 376, its worst Diwali-day reading since 2021. On Tuesday morning, the AQI hovered above 300, remaining in the "very poor" category. Authorities imposed emergency curbs on certain construction activities and older, more polluting vehicles before the festival. To blame the air crisis on fireworks alone would be missing the larger picture. Nearly every autumn and winter in recent years, emissions from automobile vehicles, factories and crop burning combine with construction dust and stagnant weather to blanket northern India in smog. Diwali is just a flashpoint in a much longer-running problem. The deeper question is why severe air pollution remains such a persistent challenge for a country making strides in renewable energy. Part of the answer lies in the difficulty of turning the expansion of clean power into a broader shift away from fossil fuels and other sources of pollution. India's solar expansion has been substantial. Installed capacity grew 38.8 percent to 135.81 gigawatts in 2025. Yet coal still accounted for about 71 percent of the country's electricity source last year, according to the International Energy Agency. That share was down from 74 percent in 2024, a sign of progress, but also a measure of how much conventional power India continues to rely on. Solar power depends on sunlight, but factories and households need reliable power around the clock. Energy storage facilities and stronger grids are essential if rising renewable capacity is to displace more coal in India. Rising electricity demand makes the transition even harder. In the first 10 months of the 2025-26 fiscal year, India added 8,810 megawatts of coal-fired capacity. For a fast-growing economy, maintaining reliable energy supply while changing its energy mix is a formidable task. China's experience offers a useful perspective, though the two countries face different conditions. Between 2013 and 2022, China's PM2.5 concentration fell 57 percent while its GDP expanded by 69 percent. Here, stricter enforcement of environmental protection measures and revamping a country's old industrial structure are of great importance. And, replacing coal-fired heating requires cleaner equipment and supporting infrastructure. Cutting vehicle emissions call for electric transportation and fast-charging networks, while tackling crop-residue burning needs machinery to collect and process agricultural waste. Making these alternatives widely available and affordable depended on manufacturing capacity, reliable supply chain and sustained investment. For India, taking emergency measures may ease severe pollution, but restrictions on construction and transportation would produce economic costs. Lasting improvements in air quality require cleaner, affordable alternatives that businesses and households could adopt, particularly as industrialization and urbanization continue. The question is how India can accelerate this transition while strengthening its manufacturing base. India has made domestic solar manufacturing a priority. Its Approved List of Models and Manufacturers framework is to extend to solar ingots and wafers from June 2028. However, in September 2025, Indian trade authorities recommended imposing anti-dumping duties on certain Chinese solar cells. Although domestic manufacturing tends to create jobs and build resilience, restrictive measures on imports would make clean-energy equipment scarcer and more costly, eventually slowing new energy transition. India should not turn its back on advanced clean technology and clean gears. This is where international cooperation could play a constructive role. China's manufacturing expertise in making batteries, electric vehicles and power storage facilities is of great help for India, which aspires to curb atmospheric pollution. As a matter of fact, China- developed clean technologies and products are welcomed by many countries in the world. In the first nine months of 2026, China's electric vehicle exports rose 72.3 percent year-on-year, lithium battery exports climbed 36.4 percent and exports of wind turbines and their components increased 22.4 percent, according to the Chinese customs authorities. The opportunities are concrete: electric two- and three-wheelers could be assembled in India, while solar and storage systems could support Indian factories, and better irrigation and crop-residue equipment could serve rural communities there. Joint ventures, component sourcing and technology partnerships could create new business opportunities for Indian businesses. Such cooperation could also help Indian companies build expertise in manufacturing, engineering, maintenance and distribution, which will also strengthen India's participation in global supply chains while supporting India's pursuit of greater industrial self-reliance. The smog is a reminder that progress in renewable energy cannot be measured by installed capacity alone. The real test is whether cleaner technologies can deliver meaningful improvements in factories, on city streets and in people's daily lives. For India, greater openness to international industrial and trade cooperation could help accelerate the new-energy transition and clean the nation's polluted air.

item.title: China's foreign trade surges 31.2% in October; imports outpace exports by 6 percentage points
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 20:45:00
A ceremony marking the arrival of the first batch of exhibits for the upcoming 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) is held at the National Exhibition and Convention Center (Shanghai), the main venue for the CIIE, in east China's Shanghai on October 26, 2026. Photo: Xinhua From surging semiconductor exports fueled by the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom to a rapidly expanding import market with diversified trading partners, China's foreign trade is gathering momentum on both sides of the ledger. Exports and imports have recorded double-digit growth for six consecutive months, with total trade surging 31.2 percent year-on-year in October and imports expanding faster than exports by 6 percentage points, according to official data released on Tuesday. Behind the impressive figures lies a more fundamental strength: China's vast and continuously upgrading manufacturing system, which has enabled the country to seize opportunities arising from global technological shifts while generating new demand and business opportunities for international partners, Chinese experts said. China's goods trade rose 20 percent year-on-year to 44.81 trillion yuan ($6.72 trillion) in the first 10 months of 2026, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC). Exports climbed 17.6 percent to 25.99 trillion yuan, while imports surged 23.6 percent to 18.82 trillion yuan. In October alone, total trade reached 4.87 trillion yuan, up 31.2 percent year-on-year, with exports rising 28.7 percent and imports jumping 34.7 percent. Huang Bin, executive dean of the Institute of Chinese Modernization at Minzu University of China, told the Global Times on Tuesday that China's sustained foreign trade growth is underpinned by its vast, comprehensive and continuously upgrading manufacturing system. He said the strength of China's industrial base has enabled the country to maintain its competitiveness in global markets and capitalize on emerging opportunities. Advanced manufacturing The strong performance of high-tech exports offers a closer look at how China's industrial upgrading and technological advances are translating into greater competitiveness in global markets. Exports of integrated circuits and memory components surged 101.9 percent and 132.5 percent, respectively, in the first 10 months, while shipments of 3D printers and industrial robots rose 104.8 percent and 17.8 percent, according to customs data. Mechanical and electrical products recorded a 25.2 percent increase to 16.81 trillion yuan, accounting for 64.7 percent of total exports, up 3.9 percentage points from a year earlier. Public data shows that China's exports are benefiting from the global AI investment boom. In October, integrated circuits exports surged 137.1 percent year-on-year in US dollar terms, while high-tech products and automatic data-processing machines recorded increases of 66.6 percent and 114.7 percent, respectively. Reuters also reported on Tuesday that global AI infrastructure investment had supported Chinese high-tech exports. Chen Jing, a vice president of the Technology and Strategy Research Institute, told the Global Times on Tuesday that rising global AI investment has boosted demand for servers, memory, optical modules, printed circuit boards, power supplies and cooling systems, creating opportunities across China's manufacturing supply chains. "China's strength is not necessarily in having the most advanced technology in every individual segment, but in its ability to deliver integrated systems," Chen said. He pointed to China's extensive industrial clusters, manufacturing scale and efficient supply chains, which allow companies to coordinate component production, testing, assembly and delivery within relatively short periods. Chen expects demand for AI-related hardware to remain resilient in 2027, with growth opportunities extending from computing equipment to power distribution, cooling systems and data center operations, although export growth may shift to a more moderate pace. Exports of China's "new three" products - electric vehicles, photovoltaic products and lithium batteries - also rose 46.5 percent in the first 10 months, highlighting the broader contribution of advanced manufacturing. Huang Bin identified three factors behind China's sustained trade growth: opportunities created by global AI investment, long-term industrial upgrading driven by the development of new quality productive forces, and diversification of trade markets. He stressed that stronger exports of electric vehicles, industrial robots and green energy products reflect years of technological accumulation rather than short-term fluctuations in overseas demand. However, Huang cautioned that the recent surge in trade value should not be equated with a corresponding increase in shipment volumes, as rising prices, particularly for AI-related products, have also contributed to the growth. He expressed cautious optimism about China's 2027 trade prospects, saying the country's industrial foundations and position in global supply chains would continue to support growth, also stressing that China will prioritize trade quality, higher-value products and domestic demand over rapid export growth and larger trade surpluses. Shared opportunities While manufacturing strength supports China's exports, the same industrial transformation is also generating fresh demand for sophisticated equipment, components and technologies from overseas. China's imports grew 23.6 percent in the first 10 months, six percentage points faster than exports. Imports of mechanical and electrical products jumped 35 percent to 8.17 trillion yuan, reflecting demand across the country's industrial sector. Notably, China recorded import growth from more than 150 countries and regions during the period, with imports from ASEAN, Latin America and Africa all reaching record highs for the same period in history. "China's vast market continues to offer opportunities for countries around the world," Lü Daliang, an official with the GAC, said on Tuesday during a press conference. The expanding demand is accompanied by increasingly diversified trading relationships. China's trade with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), its largest trading partner, rose 24.2 percent to 7.68 trillion yuan in the first 10 months. Trade with countries participating in the Belt and Road Initiative reached 22.88 trillion yuan, up 18.5 percent, while trade with the European Union increased 8.5 percent. The opportunities are also taking shape in concrete business deals. Reuters reported on November 6 that GE Aerospace signed sales and service agreements worth more than $12.9 billion in China during the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), including an agreement to supply engines for China Eastern Airlines' newly ordered Airbus aircraft. The demand also extends to sophisticated industrial equipment. Austrian machinery manufacturer WFL brought a truck-sized turn-mill machine weighing over 20 tonnes to the CIIE, which found a buyer just three days into the expo, Xinhua News Agency reported on Sunday. A company representative said China's advancing manufacturing capabilities were driving growing demand for high-end machine tools and other sophisticated industrial equipment. The six-day CIIE, which concluded in Shanghai on Tuesday, recorded $85.45 billion in intended deals calculated on a one-year basis, up 2.3 percent from the previous edition and a record high, according to Xinhua. The figures illustrate how China's expanding market is becoming a platform not only for international companies to secure orders, but also for deeper industrial cooperation and technological exchange. Huang said China's next stage of trade development should focus more on balanced growth, stronger domestic demand and continued institutional opening-up, allowing more economies to benefit from the country's development. For China, he said, the priority is always to improve the quality of trade and create more opportunities for shared growth, he added. As China's industries continue to upgrade, the country's manufacturing capabilities and expanding import demand are becoming complementary forces in global trade, connecting opportunities created by China's development with businesses and supply chains worldwide.

item.title: Justice served 28 years after rooftop murder; woman sentenced to death after years of living under a false identity
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 17:20:00
Police collect evidence at the scene of the rooftop flower-bed burial murder case in Luzhou, southwest China's Sichuan Province, on June 7, 2025. Photo: report by Xinhua News Agency A court in Southwest China's Sichuan Province on Tuesday sentenced a woman surnamed Chen to death and her ex-husband surnamed Yang to death with a two-year reprieve for the 1997 murder of a woman whose body they buried in a rooftop flower bed, according to a statement released by the Luzhou Intermediate People's Court on its official WeChat account. In its first-instance ruling, the court also found Chen guilty of forging identity documents, using false identity documents and illegally crossing borders. Taking all the offenses into account, the court sentenced her to death, deprived her of political rights for life and fined 27,000 yuan ($4,050). Yang was also deprived of political rights for life. According to the court's findings, Chen borrowed 40,000 yuan from the victim, surnamed Wu, in 1996 and agreed to repay the money before the following Chinese New Year. In early 1997, Chen proposed killing Wu to avoid repaying the debt, and Yang agreed. On February 1, 1997, Chen lured Wu to a warehouse under the pretext of repaying the debt. While Wu was counting the money, Yang strangled her to death with his hands. The couple later moved Wu's body to the rooftop and buried it in a flower bed that night. The court also found that Chen used false supporting documents to complete household registration and ID cards in May 2004, March 2011 and January 2025. Between 2008 and 2025, she used false IDs to obtain travel permits for Hong Kong, Macao and the Taiwan region, and a passport for international travel, as well as to book flights and train tickets, check into accommodation, and carry out other activities. She also illegally crossed borders on multiple occasions. After the case came to light, family members of the two defendants paid 120,000 yuan in compensation to the civil claimant. The court ruled that the conduct of both defendants constituted intentional homicide. Chen was also found to have committed three additional offenses involving forging identity documents, using false identity documents and illegally crossing borders. The court ruled that she should be sentenced for all the offenses. The court said Chen did not truthfully admit to her principal offenses after being apprehended. Given her extremely reprehensible motive, the egregious nature of the offenses and their serious consequences, the compensation paid was not sufficient grounds for a reduced sentence, the court ruled. Yang, however, was sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve in light of his confession and his good attitude toward admitting guilt and expressing remorse, the court said. The case came to light on June 7, 2025, when workers discovered human remains buried beneath a flower bed on the rooftop of a shopping complex in Luzhou, according to a report published by the Xinhua News Agency in January. Police later identified the remains as Wu's through DNA testing and tracked down Chen, who had been living in Shanghai under a false identity for years. Investigators also suspected that Chen had undergone plastic surgery to alter her appearance. Chen was taken into custody in Shanghai on September 26, 2025, and Yang was later apprehended. The investigation lasted 113 days, during which police examined nearly 50,000 archival records, according to Xinhua. Global Times

item.title: Lithuania reportedly seeks Taiwan island office renaming; Chinese expert says respect for China's core interests key to mending ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 15:13:00
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda talks to media prior the start of an EU Summit in the Europa building on June 18, 2026 in Brussels, Belgium. Photo: VCG Words alone will not mend Lithuania's fractured ties with China, a Chinese expert warned, as reports emerged that Vilnius had pressed so-called "Taiwan's Representative Office" to change its name and Lithuania's president called for normalizing diplomatic relations with Beijing. The real test, the expert said, is whether Lithuania is prepared to move beyond what he described as political opportunism and take concrete steps to respect China's core interests. Representatives of the Lithuanian Foreign Ministry presented the "Taiwanese Representative Office" with an unofficial document setting out demands, including that Taiwan change the name of its office in Vilnius, the delfi.lt news website reports. According to the website, the document was presented to the office at a meeting on September 24 attended by Deputy Foreign Minister Vidmantas Verbickas and diplomat Ričardas Šlepavičius. The document stated that the current name of the "Taiwanese Representative Office" was hindering the development of economic ties between the two sides and urged Taiwan to change it by October 1, according to delfi.lt news. Speaking with reporters, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said he had been briefed on the Lithuanian Foreign Ministry's talks with the "Taiwanese Representative Office" in Vilnius about a possible change to its name. "All matters are coordinated with me. We no longer live under the previous government, when the foreign minister [Gabrielis Landsbergis] could open a representative office simply by exchanging letters with another state, without consulting other institutions. Such nonsense no longer happens in Lithuania," Nausėda told reporters, according to Lithuanian broadcaster LRT. According to Nausėda, relations with Beijing are currently "practically zero," making the restoration of diplomatic representation the first priority, per LRT. He stressed that Lithuania wanted to normalize relations with China while maintaining good ties with the island of Taiwan. The Lithuanian government, in disregard of the Chinese side's strong objection and repeated dissuasion, approved the establishment of the so-called "Taiwanese Representative Office" in Lithuania by Taiwan authorities in August 2021. Under the one-China principle, any exchanges with China's Taiwan should be civil and non-official. By allowing the establishment of a "representative office" under the name of "Taiwanese," Vilnius has apparently reneged on the political commitments it made in the communiqué on the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Lithuania. Since then, China has adopted a slew of legitimate, reasonable and lawful countermeasures including a diplomatic downgrade between China and Lithuania. No Chinese diplomats have remained in Lithuania since May last year, according to Lithuanian media reports. Lithuania's recent signals of a willingness to improve ties with China stem largely from the realization that its previous approach to the Taiwan question has come at a cost, Jian Junbo, director of the Center for China-Europe Relations at Fudan University, told the Global Times. Jian said despite its repeated overtures, Vilnius has yet to take concrete steps toward mending relations, reflecting what the expert described as an opportunistic approach to Beijing — seeking to maintain ties with both sides without making a clear choice. The prospect of a genuine rapprochement, Jian said, ultimately hinges on whether Lithuania is prepared to respect China's core interests through concrete actions, recognize the Taiwan question as a red line for Beijing and uphold the one-China principle. In June, Nauseda told Bloomberg TV in an interview that he expected to see the first results of the country's diplomatic outreach to China within the next six months. "We'd like to normalize the political relations because those relations have been broken for a few years," Nauseda said. "We are in the process, and I hope that we will see the first results in the next six months." The onus is now on Lithuania, rather than China, to advance the normalization of bilateral relations, Jian said. While Vilnius has signaled a willingness to improve ties, meaningful progress will depend on whether it demonstrates genuine sincerity through concrete actions on the Taiwan question. Such steps could help create the political conditions needed to resolve existing differences and pave the way for a restoration of normal relations, he added. In June, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that China had repeatedly made its position clear on China-Lithuania relations. The crux of the current difficulties was that the Lithuanian side had violated the one-China principle and gone back on its political commitment made in the joint communiqué on the establishment of diplomatic relations. China remains open as always to communication, Guo said, who expressed hope that the Lithuanian side would act promptly and decisively to correct past mistakes and return to the right track of adhering to the one-China principle so as to create conditions for the normalization of relations with China.

item.title: From blank history to visual epic: How painter Shen Yaoyi walks 25,000 li to make the Long March visible
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 17:17:00
ShenYaoyi Photo: Courtesy of Shen This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March of the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army. Recently in Beijing, three Long March-themed exhibitions of works by painter Shen Yaoyi are meeting audiences. The National Museum of China's exhibition integrates original oil paintings, prints and picture-story books with digital art, creating a three-dimensional, vivid and tangible "visible Long March." The National Centre for the Performing Arts' exhibition selects oil paintings (high-definition replicas) of key moments of the Long March, capturing with rich colors those earth-shaking and heart-stirring historical instants. The Beijing Art Center's exhibition displays nearly 80 black-and-white picture-story book works that, frame by frame, unfold the long, blood-soaked expedition. Together the three exhibitions form a three-dimensional visual epic of the Long March. In an exclusive interview with the Global Times, Shen said: "The underlying tone of the Long March is heavy — blood and fire, life and death. It is the weight of history." 'Not doing it would feel like failing history' In Songzhuang, Beijing's Tongzhou district, an inconspicuous path leads to an unremarkable gate. Inside, the hawthorns in the small courtyard orchard have turned red and kiwifruits still hang on the vines. Few would imagine that deep in this almost rustic compound lies a visual "archive" of the Long March — the studio of painter Shen Yaoyi. Stepping into the studio, the space opens up. Paintings of all sizes cover the four walls — oil paintings and prints layered one upon another, resembling a small art museum. Shen led Global Times reporters toward the innermost room. On the walls, blackboards and beside the easels were pasted photographs of Red Army soldiers in various expressions and real-scene images of snow mountains and grasslands. The work he was creating still stood on the easel, with paints and brushes scattered nearby. During the interview, the word Shen mentioned most frequently was "authenticity." Authenticity is precisely the original aspiration with which he has conveyed the Long March spirit to the world through his brush. Behind it, lies the painter's long quest of measuring the Long March route with his feet and touching the temperature of history with his heart. Born in 1943, Shen, now in his eighties, still maintains the most "primitive" method of creation: the room is full of photographs, all printed out one by one and pasted up by hand so that he can look at them every day and ponder them repeatedly. "I'm not very good with those electronic things," Shen admitted. "Only when they are printed out and stuck right in front of me can the forms of each figure take root in my heart." This almost clumsy earnestness has run through most of Shen's life spent with Long March subjects. From 1988 to 2018, Shen completed the "Long March Trilogy," totaling more than 2,200 works that fully present the history of the Long March. The first part, The Red Ribbon of the Earth, mainly depicts the Central Red Army's arduous journey from the bloody battle of the Xiangjiang River to reaching Hadapu in Gansu. The text was adapted from the novel of the same name by renowned writer Wei Wei. After its publication, the work won multiple major awards and became an indispensable banner in Chinese revolutionary historical theme art creation. The second part, The Long March · 1936, and the third part, Sparks on the Journey, were both written and illustrated by Shen himself — painting first, then writing the text. In the 1980s, the picture-story book industry as a whole entered a low tide. The market shrank, creators switched professions one after another, and creating long-form picture-story books was widely regarded as a laborious task. It was against this backdrop that Shen accepted the commission for The Red Ribbon of the Earth. "Many people asked me why I took it on. Actually, there weren't that many reasons," Shen recalled. "Visual materials left from the Long March are extremely scarce; that period of history was blank in visual terms. Filling in this history was the unshirkable responsibility of art workers trained by New China." From 1988 to 1993, Shen spent six years completing The Red Ribbon of the Earth with 926 picture-story book frames, bringing the literary classic by Wei Wei to life on paper frame by frame. When asked whether, in six years of painting 926 frames, he had ever thought of giving up, he smiled and replied: "No, because you know the thing is worth doing. Not doing it would feel like failing history." Where does this sense of mission come from? Shen's answer was simple: "Our generation was trained by New China. We have a natural affinity for the Long March and revolutionary history. Artists have the responsibility to restore the historical facts of the Long March with their brushes. This is not a slogan; it is a matter of conscience." When creating The Red Ribbon of the Earth, the greatest difficulty in moving from text to image was that there was "nothing to rely on." Wei Wei's novel provided the literary skeleton, yet transforming the words into credible visual images — without photographs, without film footage, without ready visual references — meant starting almost from zero. Shen chose the clumsiest yet most solid path: retracing the Long March route. Shen Yaoyi's work on the Long March Photo: Courtesy of Shen Yaoyi Authenticity carries immense weight For The Red Ribbon of the Earth, Shen made multiple field sketching trips along the complete route of the Red Army's Long March and interviewed veteran Red Army soldiers and historical experts. "If you don't go to the sites, you cannot paint that genuine sense of exhaustion and tenacity," Shen told the Global Times. "The Long March in books is a concept; the Long March under your feet on that land is concrete." One work in the exhibitions depicts the Red Army crossing snow mountains: soldiers wrapped in thin clothing, faces purple from the cold, frost on their eyelashes, some leaning on wooden sticks, others supporting one another. The painting does not deliberately heighten tragedy, yet holds the viewer's gaze for a long time. Shen said that before creating this work he specially climbed a snow mountain to personally experience the piercing cold and the suffocating sensation of oxygen deficiency. The higher he went, the more frequently he had to stop; the entire ascent took a full eight hours. "Only by experiencing it for yourself can you appreciate the hardships of the Red Army soldiers of those years." During the interview, the reporters looked around the studio and saw old photographs of Long March figures in different poses pasted on the walls. "For real historical figures, every expression and appearance must match because if they don't, you fail them and you fail history," Shen said. On the painting table, a pair of straw sandals caught the reporters' attention. Shen said they were physical objects he had specially obtained for reference sketching. He repeatedly observed and copied the weaving texture, wear marks and the way the ties were fastened. It was precisely this obsessive attention to detail and stubborn pursuit of "authenticity" that made every scene in Shen's works stand up to scrutiny: from the way Red Army soldiers tied their straw sandals, to how troops carried their rifles on the march, to the distinctive vegetation of different terrains. Shen would repeatedly verify and revise them. In The Red Ribbon of the Earth, Shen depicted both grand battle panoramas and numerous delicate close-ups of ordinary soldiers: one mending a torn straw sandal during a brief rest on the march; another writing a letter by the light of a campfire; still another pressing his last mouthful of dry rations into a comrade's hand on a snow-capped mountain. These seemingly minor moments form the most moving warmth of the entire work. "History is created by the people, and the Long March was walked by countless ordinary soldiers. If you do not paint them, you cannot paint a true Long March." Shen told the Global Times that he has walked the Long March road with both "left foot and right foot": the "left foot" being picture-story books, the "right foot" oil paintings. "Oil painting seeks the eternity of a single moment; one painting must carry the full weight of a historical instant. Picture-story books seek the power of continuity, unfolding frame by frame so that readers follow the images through the entire journey. The two are irreplaceable." In his view, the picture-story book form is especially suited to narrating an epic like the Long March: "It can break grand history down into tangible, perceptible scenes, allowing readers to step into history page by page." In the later stages of creation, Shen felt the history of the Long March to be increasingly sacred and developed a creative complex for an "image epic." "As you paint, you feel you are not painting but conversing with history," he said. "The stories of the Red Army soldiers strike you one after another. That spiritual shock reshapes a person's values." 'When the people are painted, they come alive' After traversing the Long March route and depicting its events, what impressed Shen most deeply was "the tenacity of ordinary soldiers, their gritted-teeth perseverance every single day and every single step." Today, The Red Ribbon of the Earth has become a classic of revolutionary-themed picture-story books in the history of Chinese sequential art. Facing the younger generation, Shen's expectation is simple and sincere: "The core of the Long March spirit is never bowing one's head in the face of difficulties. Young people today need not climb snow mountains or cross grasslands, yet each has his or her own Long March. I hope what they draw from this history is that tenacity of gritted-teeth perseverance and that belief in the future." As a veteran artist who has devoted his life to revolutionary subjects, Shen also has his own thoughts on future creation of revolutionary art: "Authenticity comes first. Do not conceptualize; do not take things for granted. Go and walk, go and see, paint the genuine historical feeling, and only then can readers feel the power." "And paint people — ordinary people, their joys and sorrows. History is the history of people. When the people are painted, they come alive, and history comes alive," he stressed. As the interview ended, the reporters once again looked around Shen's studio. The straw sandals on the table remained rough and real; the unfinished work on the easel still awaited the next stroke. Shen stood in the center of the studio, his lean figure elongated by the light, resembling the marchers on the Long March road in his own paintings — neither hurried nor slow, step by step measuring the 25,000-li journey with his brush, filling a history that was almost blank in visual terms into a tangible image epic. Shen told the Global Times that the Long March can never be fully painted. "Every time I retrace the route, every time I repaint, there are new feelings. Today, I am still creating. This road, I will keep walking." As the reporters left the studio, Shen's words still echoed: "Authenticity is the life of art. A history as magnificent as the Long March deserves to be presented in the most authentic way." This is perhaps an artist's deepest tribute to that history — neither embellished nor simplified — fixing stroke by stroke a journey that winds like a red ribbon across China, forever fixed on paper and in people's hearts.
